documents.title: Fraud reference data set and label documentation

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the construction, content, representativeness and data quality of the reference data set (RDS) used to develop version 3.0 of the Payments Fraud Detection model (PFD v3.0, model inventory identifier MDL-17). It follows the RDS documentation template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A and is version-controlled in the controlled document repository. Cover block: document title "Fraud reference data set and label documentation"; model MDL-17, model version 3.0; document version 0.8; status Draft; author J. Verhoeven (Lead Data Scientist, Fraud Analytics); reviewer S. Bakker (Senior Data Scientist, Fraud Analytics); approver R. Hendriks (Director Fraud Prevention, Model Owner); approval date pending. PFD v3.0 is an internally developed gradient boosting model that scores card payments and digitally initiated credit transfers of the Bank's retail and small business customers in real time; its output is used to block, challenge or exempt payments and is therefore managed as a model under MRM-POL-001 across its full lifecycle. The scope of application comprises card-present and card-not-present authorisations on Bank-issued debit and credit cards and SEPA Credit Transfers and SEPA Instant Credit Transfers initiated through the mobile banking app and internet banking. Payments initiated through third-party payment initiation services and corporate host-to-host channels are out of scope.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS covers all in-scope payment transactions authorised or executed between 1 January 2024 and 31 December 2025, at transaction level (event-based, no snapshot aggregation). The population contains 2,914 million scored transactions (card 2,236 million; credit transfers 678 million) of 3.41 million unique customers and 4.02 million unique cards, with 71,860 confirmed fraudulent transactions (target events) with a total value of EUR 58.3 million. This corresponds to a count fraud rate of 0.25 bps and a value fraud rate of 1.6 bps over all in-scope transactions. Fraud labels were extracted on 7 April 2026, so that the most recent transaction in the window has a label maturity of 97 days.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The 24-month window balances recency against the number of fraud events. Fraud typologies change quickly: bank helpdesk (spoofing) fraud on instant payments and card-not-present account takeover via phishing increased strongly from 2023, while card skimming has become negligible after the full EMV and contactless migration. Windows longer than 24 months would over-represent typologies that are no longer relevant. The start date of 1 January 2024 also coincides with the migration of the digital banking event log to the current platform (DBEL v2), after which device and session attributes are available consistently for both channels. The data are split into development and test samples before feature selection and tuning: transactions of 2024 form the development sample and all transactions of 2025 form the out-of-time test sample, so that the test sample covers the most recent twelve months of matured outcomes.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target variable is a transaction-level binary fraud flag. A transaction is labelled fraudulent when it is confirmed as fraud through a customer fraud claim, a card scheme chargeback with a fraud reason code, or a Fraud Operations investigation, including fraud resulting from manipulation of the payer. Claims that are withdrawn, rejected after investigation or reclassified as merchant disputes are labelled genuine. A label maturity window of 90 days after the transaction date is applied to all transactions; transactions without confirmed fraud after 90 days are labelled genuine, and this window is applied consistently in development and in performance measurement. The fraud flag is aligned with the definition of fraudulent payment transactions used for the Bank's fraud reporting under EBA/GL/2018/05, so that the RDS can also be used to recompute fraud rates per transaction type under Art. 19 of the PSD2 RTS.

sections.text: Not applicable. The fraud detection model does not estimate a probability of default and does not use days-past-due counting, materiality thresholds, unlikeliness-to-pay indicators or probation periods. sections.text: Not applicable. Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers relate to the credit default definition of CR-STD-110, which is not used by this model. Customer-level events that are relevant to fraud (for example a reported lost or stolen card or a confirmed account takeover) are captured as features or label sources as described in sections 3.1 and 4.5.

sections.heading: Label construction, delay and maturity
sections.text: Labels are constructed by build job LBL-017 from the fraud case management system (FCM), the chargeback system (CBS) and the customer claims register. The reporting delay between transaction and first fraud report is short for card fraud (median 4 days) and longer for credit transfer scams (median 9 days). Across both channels, 95% of the final fraud value is reported within 41 days and 99.1% within 90 days, measured on 2023 transactions with 15 months of follow-up. Two definitions of fraud are used and labelled distinctly: FRAUD_RPT (fraud as reported to DNB under EBA/GL/2018/05, recorded on the reporting date) and FRAUD_LBL (the model label, recorded on the transaction and subject to the 90-day maturity window); the reconciliation between the two is documented in Annex A. The label construction, including the reclassification of withdrawn claims, is a defined and documented data-preparation step of the build code.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is sourced from seven data domains, each with one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue: Card Payments (card authorisation platform CAP), Payments (payments hub PHUB for SCT and SCT Inst), Digital Channels (digital banking event log DBEL v2 and the authentication platform AUTHP), Fraud (FCM and the claims register), Disputes (CBS), Customer (customer master CIF) and External Fraud Intelligence (scheme and phishing intelligence feeds). Lineage from source system to RDS field is documented for every variable, including discarded variables that are used to construct retained features, in the data dictionary in Annex A. Per variable, the lineage records the source system and fields, the intermediate stores (payments data lake raw and curated zones and the offline feature store), every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with the Airflow job or dbt model that performs it, and the extraction frequency and timing. The RDS contains the amount of each transaction in euro and original currency, the compromised-credential indicators from the scheme compromise alerts and the Bank's phishing intelligence, the malware and remote-access indicators captured by the device intelligence component of AUTHP during the authentication session and the log of use of the Bank-supplied mobile banking app and authentication app, including device binding events and abnormal use.

sections.heading: Source extraction and reconciliation
sections.text: Card authorisations are extracted daily at 02:00 from CAP, credit transfers at 02:30 from PHUB, and digital session events in near real time from DBEL through the event streaming platform into the raw zone. Labels are extracted from FCM, CBS and the claims register by the monthly job LBL-017. Data feeds used by the model are reconciled monthly with the source systems on transaction counts and values; unexplained differences above 0.1% are investigated and reported to Financial Crime Compliance. Over the 24 months of the observation window, the maximum monthly difference was 0.03% of count (card, March 2024, explained by late-arriving offline authorisations) and no unexplained difference above the 0.1% threshold occurred. The reconciliation results are part of the data quality assessment in section 6.1.2.

sections.heading: Third-party and external data
sections.text: For variables sourced from third parties, the lineage starts at the point of receipt within the Bank and records the provider, the data product and the delivery date or version: scheme compromised-account alerts (received daily through the scheme portals, product versions recorded per delivery), the phishing intelligence feed of the Bank's brand-protection provider (daily file, version 4.2) and the device intelligence risk signals of the authentication platform vendor (software development kit version recorded per event). All third-party data are delivered to and processed in data centres within the EEA; no personal data used in the RDS or in production scoring is transferred outside the EEA, and the vendor contract for the device intelligence component excludes processing outside the EEA. The fitness for use of the external feeds was assessed in the data quality assessment (EVD-17-DQR, section 4).

sections.heading: Manual interventions and lineage changes
sections.text: The RDS build contains no manual data manipulation. The only manual input is the mapping of merchant category codes (MCC) to 14 MCC risk groups, which is held as a version-controlled file in the build repository (mcc_groups_v3.csv) and documented as expert judgement EJ-17-02 under MRM-STD-023. Model data are aggregated on a fully automated basis through the scheduled build pipeline; the MCC mapping file is the only manual element and is controlled through four-eyes review of the pull request. Changes to the definition, source or transformation logic of a critical data element require the approval of the Data Owner and advance notification to the Model Owner through the data change calendar. Lineage documentation was updated before use of the data after the change of the AUTHP device-binding event schema on 14 May 2024, and the impact on the affected features was assessed and found immaterial.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Three exclusions are applied. (1) Test and staff-training transactions flagged in CAP and PHUB: 0.41 million transactions (0.01%), no fraud events. (2) Transactions with a technical decline before scoring (for example insufficient funds or invalid PIN at the terminal): 21.6 million transactions (0.74%), 212 fraud events (0.3% of events). (3) Transactions of customers deceased or in guardianship administration during the window: 3.9 million transactions (0.13%), 38 fraud events. Each exclusion is justified because the transactions are either not scored in production or not representative of the customer's own behaviour, and the impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that none of the exclusions affects representativeness. No exclusion exceeds 5% of records or value in any channel segment, so Model Owner approval of individual exclusions under MRM-STD-022 §5.3 was not required; the exclusions were nevertheless reported to Model Validation with the RDS.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per variable in Annex C and distinguishes three types: missing for a structural reason (for example no 3-D Secure data for card-present transactions, no beneficiary history for a first payment), missing at random (intermittent loss of device signals, 0.6% of sessions) and missing because of a data deficiency (web-channel malware signals before May 2024, deficiency DD-17-01). Structural missing values are encoded as a separate category; values missing at random are not imputed but passed to the gradient boosting algorithm, which learns a default split direction; the share of missing values per variable is reported in Annex C. Outliers in continuous features are identified with documented criteria (values above the 99.99th percentile of the development sample) and capped at that percentile; the same caps are stored in the feature specification and applied in the online feature store, so that development and production treatment is identical. The fraud label is never imputed: 1,184 fraud claims with an unresolved investigation status at extraction were investigated by Fraud Operations and resolved at source before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Sampling and sample definition
sections.text: Because fraud is a rare event, the modelling samples retain all fraud transactions and a stratified 2% random sample of genuine transactions (strata: channel, month and customer segment), with case weights of 50 on sampled genuine transactions so that fraud rates and value-based metrics are estimated on the full population. The development sample (2024) contains 33,940 fraud transactions and 28.0 million sampled genuine transactions; within it, 20% of customers are held out as the out-of-sample set, grouped by customer so that no customer appears in more than one sample. The out-of-time sample (2025) contains 37,920 fraud transactions and 30.2 million sampled genuine transactions. The sampling seed and strata definitions are part of the tagged build code (section 8). The sample definitions were fixed on 17 April 2026, before any feature selection or tuning.

sections.heading: Feature construction and point-in-time correctness
sections.text: All 211 candidate features are constructed point-in-time from the offline feature store, using only information with an event timestamp before the authorisation or payment initiation timestamp of the scored transaction; features derived from the fraud label, from post-transaction events or from processes triggered by the outcome (such as card blocking after a claim) are not used. Aggregation features (for example the number of card-not-present attempts in the last hour, the customer's 90-day median transfer amount or the merchant chargeback ratio over 90 days) use rolling windows closed at the transaction timestamp. A documented leakage review was performed for the four features with a univariate AUC above 0.90 or whose removal reduced model AUC by more than five percentage points; the review confirmed availability at prediction time for all four. Every feature is recorded in the Feature Register with definition, source system, lineage, transformation logic, business rationale, feature owner and availability at prediction time.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness of the development data for the current portfolio was demonstrated by comparing the development sample with all in-scope transactions of January–February 2026: the PSI of the production score of the previous model version v2.4 is 0.04 and the PSI of the ten most important features ranges from 0.01 to 0.08, all below the 0.10 amber threshold, so no feature exceeded 0.25. The appropriateness of the data for the model's range of application was also assessed qualitatively: the channel mix, the share of SEPA Instant (41% of credit transfer volume in 2025 against 28% in 2024) and the growth of card tokenised wallet payments are represented in the out-of-time sample. The fraud rate per channel differs between 2024 and 2025 (card 1.71 bps versus 1.62 bps by value; credit transfers 1.48 bps versus 1.69 bps), reflecting the shift from card to instant payment scams, which the out-of-time evaluation covers. Detailed tables per channel, amount band and customer segment are presented in Annex B.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The excluded test transactions contain no fraud and have no effect. The technically declined transactions have a fraud rate of 0.98 per 100,000 (count) against 2.47 in the retained population and are declined before scoring in production as well, so their exclusion aligns the RDS with the production scoring population. Transactions of deceased customers or customers under guardianship have a comparable feature distribution (PSI 0.03 on the ten most important features) and are excluded because transaction patterns are driven by third parties. The combined exclusions change the value fraud rate of the RDS by less than 0.01 bps. The exclusions are therefore not expected to affect representativeness.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality of the RDS was assessed before development against the dimensions completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness of MRM-STD-022, supplemented by validity and uniqueness. Completeness was measured at record level (reconciliation of transaction counts per day and channel to source) and at attribute level (share of non-missing values per feature). Consistency was assessed between the offline RDS features and the online production features (99.7% of feature values identical on a replay of 1 million transactions), over the observation period, and through logical rules between related fields. Timeliness was measured as the lag between transaction and availability of each feature at scoring time, and as the reporting delay of fraud labels. The detailed results per rule, variable and dimension, together with the number and share of excluded records by reason, are reported in the data quality assessment report EVD-17-DQR. The assessment concludes that the data are fit for the intended use and was signed off by the developer and the Model Owner on 14 April 2026, before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Data quality rules and thresholds
sections.text: Every model input and every data element used to construct the fraud label (transaction amount, timestamps, channel, fraud claim status, chargeback reason code, investigation outcome) is designated as a critical data element. Each of the 72 critical data elements has a business definition, a technical definition and at least one data quality rule per applicable mandatory dimension; where a dimension is not applicable (for example timeliness for static customer attributes), the reason is recorded. The rules are documented in Annex A of the DQ report and the recurring checks are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool under rule set DQ-MDL17. Every rule has an amber and a red threshold at least as strict as the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3; for the fraud label and the transaction amount, stricter thresholds apply (completeness red below 99.5%, reconciliation difference red above 0.1%). No threshold is less strict than the default, so no deviation approval was required. The data quality expectations for these critical data elements were agreed with the Data Owners of the Card Payments, Payments, Digital Channels and Fraud domains in the data sharing agreement DSA-2026-017.

sections.heading: Accuracy and reconciliation
sections.text: Accuracy was measured by reconciliation of transaction counts and values per day and channel to the source systems and to the payments general ledger, and by comparison of the fraud label with the independent fraud loss register of Finance. The RDS reconciles to source within 0.03% of count and 0.02% of value for every month, and the confirmed fraud value in the RDS reconciles to the fraud loss register within 0.4% (difference explained by recoveries booked after the extraction date). Critical data elements are reconciled against the source systems at least annually as part of this assessment and monthly through the feed reconciliation; unexplained differences are recorded as data quality issues. A sample of 400 labelled transactions was checked against the underlying claim and investigation files, confirming the label in 398 cases; the two errors were corrected at source in FCM.

sections.heading: Data deficiencies

sections.heading: Lawful basis and compatibility
sections.text: Production scoring is based on Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR, read with Art. 94(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/2366 and Art. 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389, which require the Bank to operate transaction monitoring to prevent and detect payment fraud; model development, validation and monitoring are based on the Bank's legitimate interest under Art. 6(1)(f). The legitimate interest assessment LIA-2025-031 of 2 December 2025 documents the purpose, the necessity of using historical transaction data to train and test the model, and the balancing against the interests of customers, taking into account pseudonymisation and the absence of other uses. Because the transaction data were collected for executing payments, the reuse for model development was assessed as compatible under Art. 6(4) GDPR: the purposes are closely linked, customers can reasonably expect fraud prevention, no special categories are processed, the consequences for customers are protective, and pseudonymisation is applied. Both lawful bases were documented before processing for v3.0 started. The processing is thereby lawful, fair and transparent towards customers, who are informed through the Bank's privacy statement.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The 24-month window balances recency against the number of fraud events. Fraud typologies change quickly: bank helpdesk (spoofing) fraud on instant payments and card-not-present account takeover via phishing increased strongly from 2023, while card skimming has become negligible after the full EMV and contactless migration. Windows longer than 24 months would over-represent typologies that are no longer relevant. The start date of 1 January 2024 also coincides with the migration of the digital banking event log to the current platform (DBEL v2), after which device and session attributes are available consistently for both channels. The data are split into development and test samples before feature selection and tuning: transactions of 2024 form the development sample and all transactions of 2025 form the out-of-time test sample, so that the test sample covers the most recent twelve months of matured outcomes.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target variable is a transaction-level binary fraud flag. A transaction is labelled fraudulent when it is confirmed as fraud through a customer fraud claim, a card scheme chargeback with a fraud reason code, or a Fraud Operations investigation, including fraud resulting from manipulation of the payer. Claims that are withdrawn, rejected after investigation or reclassified as merchant disputes are labelled genuine. A label maturity window of 90 days after the transaction date is applied to all transactions; transactions without confirmed fraud after 90 days are labelled genuine, and this window is applied consistently in development and in performance measurement. The fraud flag is aligned with the definition of fraudulent payment transactions used for the Bank's fraud reporting under EBA/GL/2018/05, so that the RDS can also be used to recompute fraud rates per transaction type under Art. 19 of the PSD2 RTS.

sections.heading: Source extraction and reconciliation
sections.text: Card authorisations are extracted daily at 02:00 from CAP, credit transfers at 02:30 from PHUB, and digital session events in near real time from DBEL through the event streaming platform into the raw zone. Labels are extracted from FCM, CBS and the claims register by the monthly job LBL-017. Data feeds used by the model are reconciled monthly with the source systems on transaction counts and values; unexplained differences above 0.1% are investigated and reported to Financial Crime Compliance. Over the 24 months of the observation window, the maximum monthly difference was 0.03% of count (card, March 2024, explained by late-arriving offline authorisations) and no unexplained difference above the 0.1% threshold occurred. The reconciliation results are part of the data quality assessment in section 6.1.2.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per variable in Annex C and distinguishes three types: missing for a structural reason (for example no 3-D Secure data for card-present transactions, no beneficiary history for a first payment), missing at random (intermittent loss of device signals, 0.6% of sessions) and missing because of a data deficiency (web-channel malware signals before May 2024, deficiency DD-17-01). Structural missing values are encoded as a separate category; values missing at random are not imputed but passed to the gradient boosting algorithm, which learns a default split direction; the share of missing values per variable is reported in Annex C. Outliers in continuous features are identified with documented criteria (values above the 99.99th percentile of the development sample) and capped at that percentile; the same caps are stored in the feature specification and applied in the online feature store, so that development and production treatment is identical. The fraud label is never imputed: 1,184 fraud claims with an unresolved investigation status at extraction were investigated by Fraud Operations and resolved at source before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Sampling and sample definition
sections.text: Because fraud is a rare event, the modelling samples retain all fraud transactions and a stratified 2% random sample of genuine transactions (strata: channel, month and customer segment), with case weights of 50 on sampled genuine transactions so that fraud rates and value-based metrics are estimated on the full population. The development sample (2024) contains 33,940 fraud transactions and 28.0 million sampled genuine transactions; within it, 20% of customers are held out as the out-of-sample set, grouped by customer so that no customer appears in more than one sample. The out-of-time sample (2025) contains 37,920 fraud transactions and 30.2 million sampled genuine transactions. The sampling seed and strata definitions are part of the tagged build code (section 8). The sample definitions were fixed on 17 April 2026, before any feature selection or tuning.

sections.heading: Feature construction and point-in-time correctness
sections.text: All 211 candidate features are constructed point-in-time from the offline feature store, using only information with an event timestamp before the authorisation or payment initiation timestamp of the scored transaction; features derived from the fraud label, from post-transaction events or from processes triggered by the outcome (such as card blocking after a claim) are not used. Aggregation features (for example the number of card-not-present attempts in the last hour, the customer's 90-day median transfer amount or the merchant chargeback ratio over 90 days) use rolling windows closed at the transaction timestamp. A documented leakage review was performed for the four features with a univariate AUC above 0.90 or whose removal reduced model AUC by more than five percentage points; the review confirmed availability at prediction time for all four. Every feature is recorded in the Feature Register with definition, source system, lineage, transformation logic, business rationale, feature owner and availability at prediction time.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness of the development data for the current portfolio was demonstrated by comparing the development sample with all in-scope transactions of January–February 2026: the PSI of the production score of the previous model version v2.4 is 0.04 and the PSI of the ten most important features ranges from 0.01 to 0.08, all below the 0.10 amber threshold, so no feature exceeded 0.25. The appropriateness of the data for the model's range of application was also assessed qualitatively: the channel mix, the share of SEPA Instant (41% of credit transfer volume in 2025 against 28% in 2024) and the growth of card tokenised wallet payments are represented in the out-of-time sample. The fraud rate per channel differs between 2024 and 2025 (card 1.71 bps versus 1.62 bps by value; credit transfers 1.48 bps versus 1.69 bps), reflecting the shift from card to instant payment scams, which the out-of-time evaluation covers. Detailed tables per channel, amount band and customer segment are presented in Annex B.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The excluded test transactions contain no fraud and have no effect. The technically declined transactions have a fraud rate of 0.98 per 100,000 (count) against 2.47 in the retained population and are declined before scoring in production as well, so their exclusion aligns the RDS with the production scoring population. sections.heading: Bias analysis of the data
sections.text: The RDS was analysed for sources of bias. Historical decision bias arises because transactions blocked by the previous model version (v2.4) were prevented and are labelled as detected fraud only when confirmed by the customer; label bias arises because fraud on customers who do not review their statements is reported later or not at all; under-representation affects customers aged 80 and over and new customers with less than three months of history; measurement bias affects the web channel, where malware signals were incomplete before May 2024. Mitigations applied: blocked transactions confirmed genuine by the customer are labelled genuine, unconfirmed blocks (0.9% of blocks) are labelled genuine unless a claim is filed within the maturity window, with a sensitivity analysis excluding them reported in MDD section 7.5, the 90-day maturity window limits late-report label bias, and the fairness analysis of the MDD (section 7.7) tests outcomes across age groups; the effect of these mitigations on performance is reported in the MDD.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality of the RDS was assessed before development against the dimensions completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness of MRM-STD-022, supplemented by validity and uniqueness. Completeness was measured at record level (reconciliation of transaction counts per day and channel to source) and at attribute level (share of non-missing values per feature). Consistency was assessed between the offline RDS features and the online production features (99.7% of feature values identical on a replay of 1 million transactions), over the observation period, and through logical rules between related fields. Timeliness was measured as the lag between transaction and availability of each feature at scoring time, and as the reporting delay of fraud labels. The detailed results per rule, variable and dimension, together with the number and share of excluded records by reason, are reported in the data quality assessment report EVD-17-DQR. The assessment concludes that the data are fit for the intended use and was signed off by the developer and the Model Owner on 14 April 2026, before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Lawful basis and compatibility
sections.text: Production scoring is based on Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR, read with Art. 94(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/2366 and Art. 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389, which require the Bank to operate transaction monitoring to prevent and detect payment fraud; model development, validation and monitoring are based on the Bank's legitimate interest under Art. 6(1)(f). The legitimate interest assessment LIA-2025-031 of 2 December 2025 documents the purpose, the necessity of using historical transaction data to train and test the model, and the balancing against the interests of customers, taking into account pseudonymisation and the absence of other uses. Because the transaction data were collected for executing payments, the reuse for model development was assessed as compatible under Art. 6(4) GDPR: the purposes are closely linked, customers can reasonably expect fraud prevention, no special categories are processed, the consequences for customers are protective, and pseudonymisation is applied. Both lawful bases were documented before processing for v3.0 started. The processing is thereby lawful, fair and transparent towards customers, who are informed through the Bank's privacy statement.

sections.heading: Special categories and protected attributes
sections.text: No special categories of personal data under Art. 9(1) GDPR are processed in the RDS. Merchant category codes that can reveal health, religious or political information (for example hospitals, religious organisations and political organisations; 23 MCCs) are aggregated into a single "other services" risk group before feature construction, so that no inference of special categories is possible from the model inputs. Protected attributes (sex, age, nationality) are not used as model features; they are held in a separate, access-restricted fairness table used only for the fairness tests of the MDD. All 64 final features were screened for proxy effects against sex and age group: no feature predicts sex with an AUC above 0.58; device operating system version age predicts the age group 65+ with an AUC of 0.67, above the 0.65 threshold, and was retained with a justification approved by the AI Governance Office on 11 June 2026 (AIGO-2026-052), because it is a direct indicator of vulnerability to overlay malware.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Annex C lists, per feature, the share of missing values in the development and out-of-time samples, the type of missingness and the treatment. Structural missing values dominate: 3-D Secure fields are missing for all card-present transactions (61% of card volume) and beneficiary history is missing for first payments to a new beneficiary (7.8% of transfers). Values missing at random are below 1% for every feature. The web-channel malware signal (DD-17-01) was missing for 29% of web sessions before 14 May 2024 and for 0.4% thereafter. Outlier caps at the 99.99th percentile affect 0.01% of values per feature; the largest effect is on the amount ratio to the customer's 90-day median, capped at 380. Re-estimating the model without caps changes the out-of-time Gini by less than 0.1 percentage points.

sections.text: Cover block: document title "Fraud model documentation"; model MDL-17 (Payments Fraud Detection), model version 3.0; document version 0.9; status Draft; author J. Verhoeven; reviewer S. Bakker; approvers R. Hendriks (Director Fraud Prevention, Model Owner) and M. de Groot (Head of Fraud Analytics, head of the modelling unit); approval date pending. PFD v3.0 scores every in-scope card authorisation and digitally initiated credit transfer in real time and returns a fraud score between 0 and 999, reason codes and a recommended action (approve, approve with transaction-risk-analysis exemption, challenge with strong customer authentication, or block and refer to Fraud Operations). It is the Bank's transaction monitoring mechanism for payment fraud under Art. 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 (PSD2 RTS), enabling the Bank to detect unauthorised or fraudulent payment transactions for the purpose of applying strong customer authentication. Intended users are the payment authorisation services (automated decision), Fraud Operations analysts (review of blocked payments) and Fraud Risk Management (strategy). Secondary use: the score is used by Fraud Risk Management for fraud rate forecasting; it is not used for customer risk rating, credit decisions or any other context. The regulatory use is fraud prevention and PSD2 transaction risk analysis (TRA). The model is Tier 2.

sections.heading: AI system assessment and AI Act classification
sections.text: PFD v3.0 was assessed against the AI system definition of Art. 3(1) AI Act: it is a machine-based system that infers from transaction and device inputs, through a model learned from data, how to generate predictions (fraud scores) and recommendations that influence payment decisions; it is therefore an AI system. The use case is classified as minimal risk under the AI Act with no transparency obligation under Art. 50: fraud detection is explicitly excluded from Annex III point 5(b), the system does not interact directly with natural persons, and it performs none of the practices prohibited by Art. 5, including social scoring. Because the use case does not fall within an Annex III area, no Art. 6(3) derogation is relied upon. The classification rationale was reviewed by the AI Governance Office on 12 November 2025. The internal AI Risk Class is Elevated, reflecting the automated blocking of customer payments, the high degree of autonomy in real-time decisions and Tier 2. sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: The model consists of three components: (1) a gradient boosting classifier producing a fraud probability from 64 features, scaled to a score of 0–999; (2) a set of 18 hard rules for known fraud scenarios maintained by Fraud Risk Management (for example card testing, SIM-swap followed by new device binding, and active phone call during a first payment to a new beneficiary); and (3) a decision layer combining score, rules and exemption eligibility into the recommended action. The transaction monitoring is based on the analysis of payment transactions and takes into account elements typical of the customer in normal use of the personalised security credentials, such as the customer's usual devices, locations, login patterns, amounts and beneficiaries. Segmentation: a single model is estimated for all channels, with channel as a feature and channel-specific thresholds, because separate models per channel performed worse on credit transfers (fewer fraud events). Dependencies: the device intelligence component of the authentication platform (malware and remote-access signals), the online feature store and the rules engine of the payment authorisation service. The model has no dependency on other models in the model inventory.

sections.heading: Coverage of the PSD2 RTS risk factors
sections.text: The model takes into account all risk factors of Art. 2(2) of the PSD2 RTS: lists of compromised or stolen authentication elements (features COMP_CRED_FLAG and CARD_COMP_ALERT from scheme compromise alerts and phishing intelligence), the amount of each transaction (AMT_EUR and amount ratios to the customer's history), known fraud scenarios (the 18 hard rules and typology features), signs of malware infection in any session of the authentication procedure (RAT_FLAG, OVERLAY_FLAG, ROOTED_FLAG) and, because the Bank supplies the mobile banking app and the authentication app, a log of their use and abnormal use (device binding age, re-installation within 24 hours, number of bound devices). For the transaction risk analysis, the model also takes into account the customer's previous spending patterns, the payment transaction history of each customer, the location of the payer (IP geolocation and, for the Bank's app, device location where consented) and of the payee (merchant country and beneficiary account country), and abnormal payment patterns relative to the customer's history. The mapping of each RTS factor to features is given in table 2.1 of this section's appendix.

sections.heading: Coverage of SIRA fraud risks
sections.text: The fraud risk scenarios of the 2026 SIRA (approved on 19 February 2026) are mapped to detection controls in the coverage matrix: the 11 material payment fraud scenarios are covered by the model score, a hard rule or both, and two scenarios are covered only partially. The gaps concern invoice fraud on business customers (modification of creditor IBAN) and purchase scams on online marketplaces, where the customer authorises a payment to a genuine account of the fraudster; both gaps are recorded with remediation plans approved by Financial Crime Compliance on 4 March 2026 (confirmation-of-payee name check signals to be added in v3.1). The intensity of the controls is commensurate with the SIRA: higher-risk channels and transaction types (instant credit transfers to new beneficiaries, card-not-present transactions at high-risk merchant groups) receive lower block thresholds than lower-risk transactions.

sections.heading: Alternatives considered and selection
sections.text: Three methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements, data, value detection rate at the operating false-positive ratio, stability over time, interpretability, latency and implementation constraints): (a) logistic regression on weight-of-evidence binned features, (b) random forest and (c) gradient boosting (LightGBM). On the out-of-time sample, the Gini coefficients were 0.884 (a), 0.921 (b) and 0.936 (c), and the card value detection rates at a false-positive ratio of 6:1 were 61.2%, 68.9% and 72.4%. The random forest exceeded the 50 ms latency budget at the 99th percentile. Gradient boosting was selected: it outperforms the transparent logistic regression by 5.2 percentage points of Gini and 11.2 percentage points of card value detection rate, which corresponds to an estimated EUR 3.1 million of additional prevented losses per year. The additional risks of the ML technique (reduced transparency, overfitting, drift sensitivity and adversarial adaptation) are addressed by monotonic constraints, SHAP-based explanations and reason codes, monthly drift monitoring and adversarial testing.

sections.heading: Variable selection
sections.text: Candidate features were assessed for economic or behavioural rationale, availability at the point of scoring within the latency budget, and stability over time (PSI between 2024 half-years below 0.10). Selection proceeded in four documented steps on the development sample only: (1) removal of 41 features failing availability or stability; (2) univariate analysis (information value and univariate AUC per channel); (3) removal of one of each pair of features with Spearman correlation above 0.85, retaining the more interpretable feature; (4) multivariate recursive elimination based on mean absolute SHAP, removing features below 1% of total mean absolute SHAP unless retained for a documented business reason. Of 211 candidates, 64 features were retained; three low-SHAP features (compromised-credential flag, rooted-device flag and SIM-swap indicator) were retained because they implement PSD2 RTS risk factors and are important for rare but severe scenarios. All features are engineered from interpretable transaction, device or behavioural concepts; no automatically generated or embedding features are used.

sections.heading: Estimation technique and hyperparameter tuning
sections.text: The classifier is a LightGBM 4.3 gradient boosting model with binary log-loss objective. The hyperparameter search space comprised the number of leaves (15–255), learning rate (0.01–0.1), minimum data in leaf (100–2,000), feature fraction (0.5–1.0), bagging fraction (0.5–1.0) and L2 regularisation (0–20); the search used Bayesian optimisation (TPE, 120 trials) with the area under the precision-recall curve on customer-grouped five-fold cross-validation within the development sample as objective and selection criterion; the test samples were never used for tuning. Selected values: 63 leaves, learning rate 0.03, minimum data in leaf 400, feature fraction 0.7, bagging fraction 0.8, L2 regularisation 5. Overfitting is controlled through L2 regularisation, minimum leaf size, row and feature subsampling, monotonic constraints and early stopping (50 rounds without improvement on the out-of-sample set), which stopped training at 487 trees. The fraud probability is corrected for the genuine-sample weighting and mapped to the score scale in chapter 5.

sections.heading: Economic rationale of drivers
sections.text: The ten most important features by mean absolute SHAP on the out-of-time sample are: amount ratio to the customer's 90-day median, beneficiary novelty and account age, active phone call during the session, device binding age, remote-access tool flag, card-not-present attempts in the last hour, merchant risk group, IP-to-usual-location distance, login-to-payment time and the compromised-credential flag. Every final driver has a direction consistent with fraud experience: higher amounts relative to history, new beneficiaries, new devices, remote access and velocity increase the score, and long customer tenure with the same device decreases it. Monotonic constraints were imposed on nine features where the direction is known a priori, and compliance with the constraints and the plausibility of the learned relationships were verified with partial dependence and ICE plots on the out-of-time sample; no implausible non-monotonic relationship was found among the unconstrained features. The dependence plots are presented in the explainability report EVD-17-XAI.

sections.heading: Score calibration and scaling
sections.text: The raw LightGBM output is converted into a population fraud probability by correcting the log-odds for the 2% genuine sampling rate (subtracting ln(50)). The probability is mapped to a score between 0 and 999 through a monotonic isotonic mapping estimated on the out-of-sample set, so that score bands correspond to stable fraud odds: at a score of 880 the observed fraud odds on the out-of-sample set are 1:6.2 for card transactions. Calibration is monitored by comparing expected and observed fraud counts per score decile; on the out-of-time sample the ratio of observed to expected fraud counts is 0.97 overall, and between 0.91 and 1.08 per decile. The calibration is used for fraud rate forecasting by Fraud Risk Management; operational decisions use the score thresholds of section 5.2.

sections.heading: Operating thresholds
sections.text: The operating thresholds were set through a documented analysis on the out-of-time sample of fraud losses prevented and the number of genuine customers affected by false positives at each candidate threshold between 800 and 950, per channel. Documented thresholds: block and refer to Fraud Operations at a score of 880 or above for card transactions and 850 or above for credit transfers to beneficiaries added in the last 24 hours (900 for other transfers); challenge with strong customer authentication between 620 and the block threshold. At the selected thresholds, the expected annual prevented loss is EUR 16.8 million and the expected number of genuine payments blocked is 165,000 per year (0.011% of transactions). The thresholds were approved by the Model Owner on 16 June 2026. Thresholds are stored in the parameter table of the decision layer and changed only through model change management.

The precision at the card block threshold is 13.9% and the recall (count) 61.8%. All metrics meet their targets.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions, parameters and input data: the label maturity window (60 and 120 days instead of 90), the genuine sampling rate (1% and 5% instead of 2%), the exclusion of unconfirmed blocks, alternative outlier caps, the removal of the device intelligence features (simulating an outage) and the calibration window. The out-of-time card value detection rate at the operating threshold changes by at most 0.4 percentage points under the alternative maturity windows and sampling rates. The removal of device intelligence features reduces the credit transfer value detection rate from 78.1% to 61.5%, which is why the fallback rules in the implementation specification apply a lower block threshold during an outage. The two expert judgements in data treatment (EJ-17-01 and EJ-17-02) and the threshold judgement (EJ-17-03) are quantified by these sensitivity analyses, with impacts of at most 0.3 percentage points of Gini.

sections.heading: Robustness and adversarial resilience
sections.text: The model achieves an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity: perturbation of continuous inputs by ±5% changes the recommended action for 0.8% of transactions near thresholds; missing, out-of-range and extreme values are handled as specified; and adversarial tests simulating evasion (amount splitting below thresholds, device spoofing without remote-access signals, slow velocity) reduce the value detection rate on the simulated attacks by at most 9 percentage points, mitigated by velocity features over 24 hours and hard rules. Risks of data poisoning (manipulated fraud claims), model extraction through probing of decline responses and model inversion were assessed with Information Security in assessment ISA-2026-033: the model is not exposed through an external interface, decline messages do not reveal scores, and labels depend on investigated claims. Details are reported in EVD-17-XAI, section 9.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions of the model were identified and assessed for plausibility: (A1) fraud labels confirmed within 90 days are complete for model training, supported by the label delay profile (99.1% of value within 90 days); (A2) the relationship between features and fraud in 2024 remains valid in the period of use, supported by the out-of-time performance in 2025; (A3) the genuine sample of 2% is representative of all genuine transactions, supported by stratification and the sampling sensitivity; (A4) device intelligence signals are available in production with the same definitions as in development, supported by the online-offline consistency test (99.7% identical); (A5) the model is used only for the in-scope channels and populations. Assumption A2 is the most uncertain because of adaptation by fraudsters; it is monitored through the monthly analysis of undetected fraud described in chapter 10.

sections.heading: Human oversight and customer impact
sections.text: Human oversight: Fraud Operations analysts review every blocked payment within the service level of 15 minutes (24/7), contact the customer through the verified app notification or telephone, and release the payment or confirm the fraud; they can override the model recommendation, and the Fraud Operations duty manager can switch the model to the fallback rule set or stop automated blocking through the decision-layer kill switch. Analysts see the score and the top three reason codes and have authority to release the payment regardless of the score; analyst releases and confirmations are monitored as overrides. A block of a payment is a decision based solely on automated processing that can significantly affect the customer. It is taken under Art. 22(2)(a) GDPR because it is necessary for the performance of the payment services contract, which obliges the Bank to prevent unauthorised payments. Customers can obtain human intervention by a Fraud Operations analyst with authority to release the payment, express their point of view and contest the block through the app or the fraud helpline, as described in procedure FO-PR-012 on customer contact and payment release. The model does not take decisions to reject credit, terminate a relationship or refuse a product.

sections.heading: Transparency towards customers and users
sections.text: Customers are informed in the Bank's privacy statement and in the payment services terms that payments are screened by automated fraud detection, including profiling of their payment behaviour, that payments may be blocked or challenged as a result, and what the main factors are (amounts, beneficiaries, devices, locations and known fraud patterns). On an access request, the Privacy Office can explain the procedure and principles applied to a specific blocked payment using the stored reason codes. Customers do not interact directly with the model; the customer contact after a block is performed by staff or by an app notification that states that the payment was stopped by the Bank's fraud detection. Internal users receive the user guide UG-PFD-3.0 describing the intended purpose, the thresholds, known limitations, performance levels and the oversight tasks expected from analysts.

Monitoring code (repository fraud-pfd-monitoring) and the monitoring data snapshots are version controlled so that results are reproducible. sections.heading: Retraining approach
sections.text: The retraining approach is defined as follows. Triggers: a red Gini or detection KPI, amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles, or a new material typology; frequency: at least every 18 months; data window: the most recent 24 months with matured labels. Pipeline elements that may change in a retraining are the training data window, the tree ensemble and the isotonic score mapping; the feature set, hyperparameter search space, label definition and thresholds may not change without a model change assessment. A retrained model must pass acceptance tests: out-of-time Gini not lower than the current model minus one percentage point, detection targets met, fairness thresholds met and online-offline reconciliation passed. Every retraining is recorded as a model change under MRM-STD-050. No continuous or online learning is used in production; the production model is a static, versioned artefact.

Verhoeven; reviewer S. Bakker; approvers R. Hendriks (Director Fraud Prevention, Model Owner) and M. de Groot (Head of Fraud Analytics, head of the modelling unit); approval date 19 June 2026. PFD v3.0 scores every in-scope card authorisation and digitally initiated credit transfer in real time and returns a fraud score between 0 and 999, reason codes and a recommended action (approve, approve with transaction-risk-analysis exemption, challenge with strong customer authentication, or block and refer to Fraud Operations). It is the Bank's transaction monitoring mechanism for payment fraud under Art. 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 (PSD2 RTS), enabling the Bank to detect unauthorised or fraudulent payment transactions for the purpose of applying strong customer authentication. Intended users are the payment authorisation services (automated decision), Fraud Operations analysts (review of blocked payments) and Fraud Risk Management (strategy). Secondary use: the score is used by Fraud Risk Management for fraud rate forecasting; it is not used for customer risk rating, credit decisions or any other context. The regulatory use is fraud prevention and PSD2 transaction risk analysis (TRA). The model is Tier 2.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: The model consists of three components: (1) a gradient boosting classifier producing a fraud probability from 64 features, scaled to a score of 0–999; (2) a set of 18 hard rules for known fraud scenarios maintained by Fraud Risk Management (for example card testing, SIM-swap followed by new device binding, and active phone call during a first payment to a new beneficiary); and (3) a decision layer combining score, rules and exemption eligibility into the recommended action. The transaction monitoring is based on the analysis of payment transactions and takes into account elements typical of the customer in normal use of the personalised security credentials, such as the customer's usual devices, locations, login patterns, amounts and beneficiaries. Segmentation: a single model is estimated for all channels, with channel as a feature and channel-specific thresholds, because separate models per channel performed worse on credit transfers (fewer fraud events). Dependencies: the device intelligence component of the authentication platform (malware and remote-access signals), the online feature store and the rules engine of the payment authorisation service. The model has no dependency on other models in the model inventory.

sections.heading: Coverage of the PSD2 RTS risk factors
sections.text: The model takes into account all risk factors of Art. 2(2) of the PSD2 RTS: lists of compromised or stolen authentication elements (features COMP_CRED_FLAG and CARD_COMP_ALERT from scheme compromise alerts and phishing intelligence), the amount of each transaction (AMT_EUR and amount ratios to the customer's history), known fraud scenarios (the 18 hard rules and typology features), signs of malware infection in any session of the authentication procedure (RAT_FLAG, OVERLAY_FLAG, ROOTED_FLAG) and, because the Bank supplies the mobile banking app and the authentication app, a log of their use and abnormal use (device binding age, re-installation within 24 hours, number of bound devices). For the transaction risk analysis, the model also takes into account the customer's previous spending patterns, the payment transaction history of each customer, the location of the payer (IP geolocation and, for the Bank's app, device location where consented) and of the payee (merchant country and beneficiary account country), and abnormal payment patterns relative to the customer's history. The mapping of each RTS factor to features is given in table 2.1 of this section's appendix.

sections.heading: Coverage of SIRA fraud risks
sections.text: The fraud risk scenarios of the 2026 SIRA (approved on 19 February 2026) are mapped to detection controls in the coverage matrix: the 11 material payment fraud scenarios are covered by the model score, a hard rule or both, and two scenarios are covered only partially. The gaps concern invoice fraud on business customers (modification of creditor IBAN) and purchase scams on online marketplaces, where the customer authorises a payment to a genuine account of the fraudster; both gaps are recorded with remediation plans approved by Financial Crime Compliance on 4 March 2026 (confirmation-of-payee name check signals to be added in v3.1). The intensity of the controls is commensurate with the SIRA: higher-risk channels and transaction types (instant credit transfers to new beneficiaries, card-not-present transactions at high-risk merchant groups) receive lower block thresholds than lower-risk transactions.

sections.heading: Alternatives considered and selection
sections.text: Three methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements, data, value detection rate at the operating false-positive ratio, stability over time, interpretability, latency and implementation constraints): (a) logistic regression on weight-of-evidence binned features, (b) random forest and (c) gradient boosting (LightGBM). On the out-of-time sample, the Gini coefficients were 0.884 (a), 0.921 (b) and 0.936 (c), and the card value detection rates at a false-positive ratio of 6:1 were 61.2%, 68.9% and 72.4%. The random forest exceeded the 50 ms latency budget at the 99th percentile. Gradient boosting was selected: it outperforms the transparent logistic regression by 5.2 percentage points of Gini and 11.2 percentage points of card value detection rate, which corresponds to an estimated EUR 3.1 million of additional prevented losses per year. The additional risks of the ML technique (reduced transparency, overfitting, drift sensitivity and adversarial adaptation) are addressed by monotonic constraints, SHAP-based explanations and reason codes, monthly drift monitoring and adversarial testing.

sections.heading: Variable selection
sections.text: Candidate features were assessed for economic or behavioural rationale, availability at the point of scoring within the latency budget, and stability over time (PSI between 2024 half-years below 0.10). Selection proceeded in four documented steps on the development sample only: (1) removal of 41 features failing availability or stability; (2) univariate analysis (information value and univariate AUC per channel); (3) removal of one of each pair of features with Spearman correlation above 0.85, retaining the more interpretable feature; (4) multivariate recursive elimination based on mean absolute SHAP, removing features below 1% of total mean absolute SHAP unless retained for a documented business reason. Of 211 candidates, 64 features were retained; three low-SHAP features (compromised-credential flag, rooted-device flag and SIM-swap indicator) were retained because they implement PSD2 RTS risk factors and are important for rare but severe scenarios. All features are engineered from interpretable transaction, device or behavioural concepts; no automatically generated or embedding features are used.

sections.heading: Estimation technique and hyperparameter tuning
sections.text: The classifier is a LightGBM 4.3 gradient boosting model with binary log-loss objective. The hyperparameter search space comprised the number of leaves (15–255), learning rate (0.01–0.1), minimum data in leaf (100–2,000), feature fraction (0.5–1.0), bagging fraction (0.5–1.0) and L2 regularisation (0–20); the search used Bayesian optimisation (TPE, 120 trials) with the area under the precision-recall curve on customer-grouped five-fold cross-validation within the development sample as objective and selection criterion; the test samples were never used for tuning. Selected values: 63 leaves, learning rate 0.03, minimum data in leaf 400, feature fraction 0.7, bagging fraction 0.8, L2 regularisation 5. Overfitting is controlled through L2 regularisation, minimum leaf size, row and feature subsampling, monotonic constraints and early stopping (50 rounds without improvement on the out-of-sample set), which stopped training at 487 trees. The fraud probability is corrected for the genuine-sample weighting and mapped to the score scale in chapter 5.

sections.heading: Economic rationale of drivers
sections.text: The ten most important features by mean absolute SHAP on the out-of-time sample are: amount ratio to the customer's 90-day median, beneficiary novelty and account age, active phone call during the session, device binding age, remote-access tool flag, card-not-present attempts in the last hour, merchant risk group, IP-to-usual-location distance, login-to-payment time and the compromised-credential flag. Every final driver has a direction consistent with fraud experience: higher amounts relative to history, new beneficiaries, new devices, remote access and velocity increase the score, and long customer tenure with the same device decreases it. Monotonic constraints were imposed on nine features where the direction is known a priori, and compliance with the constraints and the plausibility of the learned relationships were verified with partial dependence and ICE plots on the out-of-time sample; no implausible non-monotonic relationship was found among the unconstrained features. The dependence plots are presented in the explainability report EVD-17-XAI.

sections.heading: Score calibration and scaling
sections.text: The raw LightGBM output is converted into a population fraud probability by correcting the log-odds for the 2% genuine sampling rate (subtracting ln(50)). The probability is mapped to a score between 0 and 999 through a monotonic isotonic mapping estimated on the out-of-sample set, so that score bands correspond to stable fraud odds: at a score of 880 the observed fraud odds on the out-of-sample set are 1:6.2 for card transactions. Calibration is monitored by comparing expected and observed fraud counts per score decile; on the out-of-time sample the ratio of observed to expected fraud counts is 0.97 overall, and between 0.91 and 1.08 per decile. The calibration is used for fraud rate forecasting by Fraud Risk Management; operational decisions use the score thresholds of section 5.2.

sections.heading: Operating thresholds
sections.text: The operating thresholds were set through a documented analysis on the out-of-time sample of fraud losses prevented and the number of genuine customers affected by false positives at each candidate threshold between 800 and 950, per channel. Documented thresholds: block and refer to Fraud Operations at a score of 880 or above for card transactions and 850 or above for credit transfers to beneficiaries added in the last 24 hours (900 for other transfers); challenge with strong customer authentication between 620 and the block threshold. At the selected thresholds, the expected annual prevented loss is EUR 16.8 million and the expected number of genuine payments blocked is 165,000 per year (0.011% of transactions). The thresholds were approved by the Model Owner on 16 June 2026. Thresholds are stored in the parameter table of the decision layer and changed only through model change management.

sections.heading: Transaction risk analysis exemption and fraud rates
sections.text: The Bank uses the transaction-risk-analysis (TRA) exemption of Art. 18 of the PSD2 RTS for remote card-based payments as issuer, for transactions up to an exemption threshold value of EUR 100, where the reference fraud rate in the Annex is 0.13% (13 bps). A transaction is exempted only if the model score is below 310, no hard rule is triggered and none of the Art. 18(2)(c) signals is present: abnormal spending or behavioural pattern, unusual device or software access, malware infection in any session of the authentication procedure, a known fraud scenario, an abnormal location of the payer or a high-risk location of the payee. The fraud rate per transaction type is calculated as the total value of unauthorised or fraudulent remote transactions, recovered or not, divided by the total value of all remote transactions of the same type, including those authenticated with SCA and those executed under an exemption, on a rolling quarterly (90-day) basis. The Bank's remote card fraud rate was 5.2 bps in 2025, well below 13 bps. The remote credit transfer fraud rate (1.6 bps) exceeds the 1.5 bps reference rate of the lowest band, so the exemption is not used for credit transfers. Fraud rates, fraud and total values, average transaction values and the number and share of transactions per exemption are recorded and monitored quarterly per payment type, split remote and non-remote. Where the monitored fraud rate exceeds the reference fraud rate for two consecutive quarters, the exemption is switched off immediately through the decision-layer parameter TRA_ENABLED. The methodology, the model and the reported fraud rates are audited yearly by Group Audit, whose last review was completed on 28 November 2025. This documentation, including the fraud rate calculation code (repository fraud-tra-reporting), is available to DNB and the EBA on request.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power and detection performance
sections.text: Performance was tested on the development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples for discriminatory power (Gini and area under the precision-recall curve), calibration accuracy (observed to expected fraud counts) and stability, using the metrics and thresholds of MV-HB-003. Gini: development 0.951, out-of-sample 0.945, out-of-time 0.936; the Gini gap between development and out-of-time samples is 1.5 percentage points, well below the five-percentage-point justification threshold. At the operating thresholds on the out-of-time sample, per payment channel against the documented targets: card count detection rate 61.8% (target at least 55%), card value detection rate 72.4% (target at least 65%), card false-positive ratio 6.2:1 (target at most 8:1); credit transfer count detection rate 58.3% (target at least 50%), value detection rate 78.1% (target at least 70%), false-positive ratio 11.4:1 (target at most 15:1). The precision at the card block threshold is 13.9% and the recall (count) 61.8%. All metrics meet their targets.

sections.text: Performance was tested for the whole model and for each material segment: channel (card-present, card-not-present, SCT, SCT Inst), customer segment (retail, private banking, small business), amount band and fraud typology. Out-of-time Gini by channel: card-present 0.901, card-not-present 0.944, SCT 0.922, SCT Inst 0.931. sections.heading: Benchmarking and challenger comparison
sections.text: As a Tier 2 model, v3.0 is compared with the previous model version v2.4 as benchmark: on the out-of-time sample, v2.4 achieves a Gini of 0.912 and a card value detection rate of 66.0% at the same false-positive ratio, against 0.936 and 72.4% for v3.0. sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions, parameters and input data: the label maturity window (60 and 120 days instead of 90), the genuine sampling rate (1% and 5% instead of 2%), the exclusion of unconfirmed blocks, alternative outlier caps, the removal of the device intelligence features (simulating an outage) and the calibration window. The out-of-time card value detection rate at the operating threshold changes by at most 0.4 percentage points under the alternative maturity windows and sampling rates. The removal of device intelligence features reduces the credit transfer value detection rate from 78.1% to 61.5%, which is why the fallback rules in the implementation specification apply a lower block threshold during an outage. The two expert judgements in data treatment (EJ-17-01 and EJ-17-02) and the threshold judgement (EJ-17-03) are quantified by these sensitivity analyses, with impacts of at most 0.3 percentage points of Gini.

sections.heading: Fairness
sections.text: Fairness was tested before approval on the out-of-time sample across sex and age group (18–34, 35–49, 50–64, 65 and over), which are lawfully available from the customer master for this purpose; nationality was not tested because it is not processed for fraud prevention. The favourable outcome is a genuine payment that is not blocked. The ratio of favourable-outcome rates between the least and most favoured group is 0.9987 for age group and 0.9998 for sex, above the 0.80 threshold. The difference in true-positive rates (count detection rate) is 1.9 percentage points between sexes and 6.7 percentage points between age groups (60.2% for 18–34 against 66.9% for 65 and over), which exceeds the five-percentage-point threshold; calibration by group (observed to expected fraud counts 0.93–1.04) is reported. The root cause analysis attributes the age-group difference to typology mix: younger customers are more exposed to purchase scams and social-media-initiated fraud with genuine-looking behaviour, older customers to bank helpdesk fraud with strong session signals. Within typology the difference is below 2 percentage points. The retention was approved by the AI Governance Office on 11 June 2026 (AIGO-2026-052) with monthly monitoring by age group. These procedures ensure that the profiling uses appropriate statistical procedures, corrects factors resulting in inaccuracies and prevents discriminatory effects.

sections.text: The model achieves an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity: perturbation of continuous inputs by ±5% changes the recommended action for 0.8% of transactions near thresholds; missing, out-of-range and extreme values are handled as specified; and adversarial tests simulating evasion (amount splitting below thresholds, device spoofing without remote-access signals, slow velocity) reduce the value detection rate on the simulated attacks by at most 9 percentage points, mitigated by velocity features over 24 hours and hard rules. Risks of data poisoning (manipulated fraud claims), model extraction through probing of decline responses and model inversion were assessed with Information Security in assessment ISA-2026-033: the model is not exposed through an external interface, decline messages do not reveal scores, and labels depend on investigated claims. Details are reported in EVD-17-XAI, section 9.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions of the model were identified and assessed for plausibility: (A1) fraud labels confirmed within 90 days are complete for model training, supported by the label delay profile (99.1% of value within 90 days); (A2) the relationship between features and fraud in 2024 remains valid in the period of use, supported by the out-of-time performance in 2025; (A3) the genuine sample of 2% is representative of all genuine transactions, supported by stratification and the sampling sensitivity; (A4) device intelligence signals are available in production with the same definitions as in development, supported by the online-offline consistency test (99.7% identical); (A5) the model is used only for the in-scope channels and populations. Assumption A2 is the most uncertain because of adaptation by fraudsters; it is monitored through the monthly analysis of undetected fraud described in chapter 10.

sections.heading: Human oversight and customer impact
sections.text: Human oversight: Fraud Operations analysts review every blocked payment within the service level of 15 minutes (24/7), contact the customer through the verified app notification or telephone, and release the payment or confirm the fraud; they can override the model recommendation, and the Fraud Operations duty manager can switch the model to the fallback rule set or stop automated blocking through the decision-layer kill switch. Analysts see the score and the top three reason codes and have authority to release the payment regardless of the score; analyst releases and confirmations are monitored as overrides. A block of a payment is a decision based solely on automated processing that can significantly affect the customer. It is taken under Art. 22(2)(a) GDPR because it is necessary for the performance of the payment services contract, which obliges the Bank to prevent unauthorised payments. Customers can obtain human intervention by a Fraud Operations analyst with authority to release the payment, express their point of view and contest the block through the app or the fraud helpline, as described in procedure FO-PR-012 on customer contact and payment release. The model does not take decisions to reject credit, terminate a relationship or refuse a product.

sections.heading: Transparency towards customers and users
sections.text: Customers are informed in the Bank's privacy statement and in the payment services terms that payments are screened by automated fraud detection, including profiling of their payment behaviour, that payments may be blocked or challenged as a result, and what the main factors are (amounts, beneficiaries, devices, locations and known fraud patterns). Customers do not interact directly with the model; the customer contact after a block is performed by staff or by an app notification that states that the payment was stopped by the Bank's fraud detection. Internal users receive the user guide UG-PFD-3.0 describing the intended purpose, the thresholds, known limitations, performance levels and the oversight tasks expected from analysts.

sections.heading: Frequency, reporting and escalation

sections.heading: Retraining approach
sections.text: The retraining approach is defined as follows. Triggers: a red Gini or detection KPI, amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles, or a new material typology; frequency: at least every 18 months; data window: the most recent 24 months with matured labels. Pipeline elements that may change in a retraining are the training data window, the tree ensemble and the isotonic score mapping; the feature set, hyperparameter search space, label definition and thresholds may not change without a model change assessment. A retrained model must pass acceptance tests: out-of-time Gini not lower than the current model minus one percentage point, detection targets met, fairness thresholds met and online-offline reconciliation passed. Every retraining is recorded as a model change under MRM-STD-050. No continuous or online learning is used in production; the production model is a static, versioned artefact.

sections.text: Global feature importance was computed as the mean absolute TreeSHAP value on the out-of-time sample and cross-checked with permutation importance on the value detection rate; the rank correlation between both methods for the top 20 features is 0.88. The five most important features account for 41% of total mean absolute SHAP: amount ratio to the customer's 90-day median (11.8%), beneficiary novelty and account age (9.6%), active phone call during the session (7.4%), device binding age (6.3%) and remote-access tool flag (5.9%). Fraud Operations and Fraud Risk Management reviewed the ranking in a workshop on 28 May 2026 and confirmed that the main drivers are consistent with their experience of current typologies.

deficiencies.rationale: MDD section 5.2 documents the threshold analysis of prevented fraud losses and genuine payments blocked, but the operational capacity of Fraud Operations (case volumes against the 15-minute review service level) is not analysed, and the thresholds are approved by the Model Owner only, without the required approval of Fraud Risk Management.

mitigation.text: Add a capacity analysis of expected blocked-payment volumes per hour against Fraud Operations staffing, and obtain and record the approval of Fraud Risk Management for the operating thresholds.

deficiencies.rationale: RDS section 4.3 and Annex C report the share of missing values per feature and state that values missing at random are passed to the algorithm's default split direction, but the effect of this treatment on the estimated model is not assessed (for example against explicit imputation or a missing-indicator variant for the device intelligence signals, which are missing for 0.6% of sessions and up to 2.8% in the web channel).

mitigation.text: Quantify the effect of the missing-value treatment on out-of-time Gini and detection rates by comparing it with at least one explicit imputation method, and document the result in RDS Annex C.

deficiencies.rationale: The user guide UG-PFD-3.0 is referenced, but the documentation does not show that it states the performance levels (detection rates and false-positive ratios per channel) and the known limitations (LIM-17-01 to LIM-17-06) that Fraud Operations analysts need for their oversight tasks.

mitigation.text: Extend the user guide with performance levels per channel and the limitations log extract, and reference the updated guide version in MDD section 9.2.

deficiencies.rationale: The RDS documentation states that all features are constructed point-in-time. Independent replication shows that the offline feature merchant_cb_ratio_90d counts chargebacks by posting date up to the snapshot load date rather than up to the transaction timestamp, so chargebacks raised after the scored transaction (including those on the transaction itself) enter the feature. Rebuilding the feature point-in-time lowers the out-of-time card value detection rate from 72.4% to 70.6%.

mitigation.text: Rebuild merchant_cb_ratio_90d with an event-time cut-off at the transaction timestamp, retrain and re-evaluate the model, and add an automated point-in-time test for all aggregation features to the build pipeline.

deficiencies.rationale: A uniform 90-day label maturity window is documented and justified with a delay profile measured on 2023 transactions (99.1% of fraud value within 90 days), when card fraud dominated. Model Validation's analysis by channel on Q1 2025 transactions with at least 15 months of follow-up shows that for credit transfer scams 8.6% of the ultimate fraud value is reported after day 90 (against 0.4% for card fraud), so credit transfer labels in the last quarter of the out-of-time sample are incomplete and the credit transfer detection rates and remote credit transfer fraud rates are overstated by about 1.5 percentage points.

mitigation.text: Set a channel-specific maturity window for credit transfers (at least 150 days) based on the observed delay profile, restate the out-of-time credit transfer metrics, and apply the window in monitoring.
